entries.title: Two Regions — A and B
entries.example: The same mark position (for example, marking the port edge of a channel when approaching from seaward) will be a RED can in Europe, but a GREEN can in the USA: it is the same type of mark (port-hand lateral mark), but the colouring depends on the region.
commentary: The IALA Maritime Buoyage System operates in two regions, which differ ONLY in the colour and shape of LATERAL marks (all other mark types — cardinal marks, isolated danger marks, safe water marks, special marks — are the same in both regions).
Region A: Europe, Africa, most of Asia, Australia, New Zealand.
Region B: North and South America, Japan, Republic of Korea, the Philippines.

The direction of buoyage is established by the authority responsible for the waters concerned — generally from seaward towards the harbour/river/estuary, or clockwise around a continent (where there is no obvious port approach).

entries.title: Port Hand Mark (Region A)
entries.example: Entering harbour from seaward in the Baltic Sea (Region A), the navigator leaves red can-shaped marks to port.
commentary: Colour: RED.
Shape: cylindrical (can).
Topmark (if fitted): single red can.
Light (if fitted): red, any rhythm.
When proceeding in the direction of buoyage, this mark is left to PORT.

entries.title: Starboard Hand Mark (Region A)
entries.example: Entering harbour from seaward in the Baltic Sea (Region A), the navigator leaves green conical marks to starboard.
commentary: Colour: GREEN.
Shape: conical (nun).
Topmark (if fitted): single green cone.
Light (if fitted): green, any rhythm.
When proceeding in the direction of buoyage, this mark is left to STARBOARD.

entries.title: Port Hand Mark (Region B)
entries.example: Entering harbour on the US East Coast (Region B), the navigator leaves green can-shaped marks to port — the colour being the opposite of Europe.
commentary: Colour: GREEN (opposite of Region A).
Shape: cylindrical (can) — the shape for the same side is retained, only the colour changes.
Light (if fitted): green.
When proceeding in the direction of buoyage, this mark is left to PORT.

entries.title: Starboard Hand Mark (Region B)
entries.example: Entering harbour on the US East Coast (Region B), the navigator leaves red conical marks to starboard.
commentary: Colour: RED (opposite of Region A).
Shape: conical (nun).
Light (if fitted): red.
When proceeding in the direction of buoyage, this mark is left to STARBOARD.

entries.title: Purpose and General Colouring
entries.example: If a cardinal mark stands beside an isolated shoal and is marked as a north cardinal mark, the safe passage for a vessel lies to the north of the mark, while the shoal/danger itself lies to the south of it.
commentary: A cardinal mark indicates on which side of it safe water lies: the name of the mark corresponds to the compass quadrant in which it is safe to pass. A north mark is passed to the north of it, a south mark to the south of it, and so on.
Shape: pillar or spar, fitted with a topmark of TWO BLACK CONES (the arrangement of the cones is the primary means of identification — see the following entries).

Lights (if fitted) are ALWAYS white, quick or very quick flashing, and are distinguished from one another by the number of flashes in each group (mnemonic — like the hands of a clock: east≈3 o'clock, south≈6 o'clock, west≈9 o'clock).

entries.title: North (N) Cardinal Mark
commentary: Topmark: two black cones, BOTH points upward (one above the other).
Colouring: black above yellow.
Light: white, continuous quick flashing or very quick flashing (Q or VQ, uninterrupted within the group).

entries.title: South (S) Cardinal Mark
commentary: Topmark: two black cones, BOTH points downward (one below the other).
Colouring: yellow above black (opposite of the North mark).
Light: white, group of 6 quick flashes plus one LONG flash (the long flash is the distinguishing feature of the South mark, to prevent confusion with the continuous flashing of the North mark).

entries.title: East (E) Cardinal Mark
commentary: Topmark: two black cones base to base (the widest part in the middle — the silhouette resembles a diamond).
Colouring: black-yellow-black (three horizontal bands, with a narrow yellow band in the middle).
Light: white, group of 3 quick flashes (mnemonic — "3 o'clock" on a clock face).

entries.title: West (W) Cardinal Mark
commentary: Topmark: two black cones point to point (the narrowest part in the middle — the silhouette resembles a wine glass, mnemonic "W = Wine glass").
Colouring: yellow-black-yellow (three horizontal bands, with a narrow black band in the middle).
Light: white, group of 9 quick flashes (mnemonic — "9 o'clock" on a clock face).

entries.title: Isolated Danger Mark
commentary: Erected directly over an isolated danger of limited extent, with navigable water all around it.
Colouring: black with one or more broad red horizontal bands.
Topmark: two black spheres, one above the other.
Light (if fitted): white, group flashing (2) — Fl(2).

entries.title: Safe Water Mark
commentary: Indicates that there is navigable water all around the mark (for example, on the centreline of a fairway, or as a landfall buoy marking the start of a fairway).
Colouring: red and white vertical stripes.
Shape: spherical, or a pillar/spar fitted with a single red spherical topmark.
Light (if fitted): white, isophase, occulting, one long flash every 10 seconds, or Morse "A" (short-long).

entries.title: Special Mark
commentary: Does not indicate a navigational danger, but marks a special area or feature: a spoil ground, a submarine cable or pipeline, a military exercise zone, a recreational zone, an ODAS buoy, etc. — the exact purpose should be checked against the chart or Notices to Mariners.
Colouring: yellow.
Topmark (if fitted): a single yellow X-shape (a saltire).
Light (if fitted): yellow, any rhythm not reserved for the white lights of cardinal, isolated danger, or safe water marks (Fl.Y is commonly used).

entries.title: Emergency Wreck Marking Buoy
commentary: A relatively new type of mark (introduced by IALA in the 2000s) — laid temporarily over a new wreck or obstruction not yet shown on the chart, until a survey or clearance has been carried out.
Colouring: alternating blue and yellow vertical stripes in equal numbers (4 to 8 stripes).
Topmark: yellow upright cross (St George's cross, NOT a diagonal St Andrew's cross) — the only topmark authorised for this mark.
Light: rhythm Oc(2)Al.BY — blue 1s, dark 0.5s, yellow 1s, dark 0.5s, the cycle repeating every 3s. No other mark uses blue colouring or a blue light — the combination is unambiguously identifiable.
In practice encountered less often than the classic marks — not to be confused with the (yellow) special mark.
